questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a mineral from a rock?
options: A mineral has a definite composition and crystal structure; a rock is an aggregate of minerals
A mineral is any solid that can be mined at a profit; a rock is a solid that cannot be mined at a profit
A mineral is formed only by living organisms; a rock is formed only by cooling of magma or lava
A mineral is always a pure chemical element; a rock is always a mixture of two or more compounds
questions.explanation: Minerals are naturally occurring, inorganic solids with a definite composition and an ordered crystal structure, and rocks are made of one or more minerals. Profitability defines an ore, not a mineral, and most minerals are compounds rather than elements.

questions.stem: What makes a rock an ore?
options: It formed deep underground under very high temperature and high pressure
It is made of a single mineral rather than a mixture of different minerals
It contains a valuable mineral concentrated enough to be mined at a profit
It contains at least one metallic element somewhere in its crystal structure
questions.explanation: An ore is defined economically: it holds a useful mineral at a grade that can be extracted at a profit with current technology and prices. Many rocks contain metals at concentrations far too low to be worth mining.

questions.stem: A rock contains 0.4% copper. When the copper price doubles, a company starts mining it, although it had been left in the ground for years. What does this show about ores?
options: The rock changed composition once mining began, which raised its copper grade
Copper minerals only become ores once they have been exposed by surface weathering
A rock becomes an ore when its copper content passes a fixed legal limit of 0.4%
Whether a rock is an ore depends on prices and costs, not only on its composition
questions.explanation: The rock itself did not change; the higher price made extraction profitable, so it became an ore. The boundary between ore and waste rock shifts with commodity prices, extraction costs and technology.

questions.stem: Compared with felsic minerals, mafic minerals are richer in which elements?
options: Silicon and oxygen
Aluminium and potassium
Magnesium and iron
Sodium and potassium
questions.explanation: Mafic comes from magnesium and ferric (iron), and mafic minerals such as olivine and pyroxene are rich in both. Felsic minerals such as quartz and potassium feldspar are richer in silica, sodium, potassium and aluminium.

questions.stem: Which group contains only felsic minerals?
options: Quartz, olivine and pyroxene
Amphibole, olivine and muscovite
Quartz, potassium feldspar and muscovite
Olivine, pyroxene and calcium-rich plagioclase
questions.explanation: Quartz, potassium feldspar and muscovite are silica-rich and pale, and they dominate felsic rocks such as granite. Olivine and pyroxene are mafic minerals rich in magnesium and iron.

questions.stem: Which comparison of mafic and felsic magma is correct?
options: Mafic magma has less silica, is hotter and flows more easily than felsic magma
Mafic magma has more silica, is cooler and is more viscous than felsic magma
Mafic magma has less silica, is cooler and is more viscous than felsic magma
Mafic magma has more silica, is hotter and flows more easily than felsic magma
questions.explanation: Silica forms linked chains in a melt, so silica-rich felsic magma is stiff and viscous, and it also melts at lower temperatures. Low-silica mafic magma is hotter and runny, which is why basalt lava forms long flows.

questions.stem: At a mid-ocean ridge, mantle rock rises and partially melts as the pressure on it falls. Which magma type and rock form there?
options: Mafic magma, which forms basalt and gabbro
Felsic magma, which forms granite and rhyolite
Mafic magma, which forms granite and rhyolite
Felsic magma, which forms basalt and gabbro
questions.explanation: Partial melting of the mantle at divergent boundaries produces low-silica mafic magma, which forms basalt at the surface and gabbro below. That is why the oceanic crust is mafic.

questions.stem: Volcanoes in the Andes, above an ocean plate subducting beneath South America, erupt magma with more silica than the basalt erupted at mid-ocean ridges. What best explains this?
options: The subducting ocean plate is made of felsic rock that melts directly into magma
Seawater dissolves silica into the magma as the plate descends into the trench
The magma cools faster than ridge magma, which raises the silica it contains
Magma from the mantle wedge melts and mixes with continental crust as it rises
questions.explanation: Water released from the subducting slab lowers the melting point of the mantle wedge, and the magma produced rises through thick continental crust, melting and absorbing silica-rich rock. The ocean plate itself is basaltic, so it cannot supply felsic magma directly.

questions.stem: Where two continental plates collide, granite bodies often form deep in the thickened crust. What type of magma forms these granites?
options: Mafic magma rising from a deep mantle hotspot
Felsic magma from melting of continental crust
Mafic magma from melting of the upper mantle
Felsic magma from melting of the oceanic crust
questions.explanation: Continental collision thickens the crust until its lower parts are hot enough to partly melt, giving silica-rich felsic magma that crystallises as granite. Little mantle-derived mafic magma reaches the surface in collision zones.

questions.stem: In a mineral identification test, what is the streak of a mineral?
options: The colour of its powder when rubbed on unglazed porcelain
The way light reflects from the surface of a fresh crystal
The pattern of flat surfaces formed when the mineral breaks
The colour of the mineral when it is held up to the light
questions.explanation: Streak is the colour of a mineral's powder, produced by scraping it across an unglazed porcelain plate. It is more reliable than the colour of the sample, which can vary with impurities and weathering; how light reflects is lustre.

questions.stem: A pale mineral scratches glass, shows no cleavage and breaks with curved, shell-like surfaces. A dichotomous key leads to which mineral?
options: Orthoclase feldspar
Quartz
Calcite
Muscovite
questions.explanation: Quartz has a hardness of 7, so it scratches glass, and it has no cleavage, breaking with conchoidal fracture instead. Orthoclase is also hard but has two good cleavages, and calcite and muscovite are too soft to scratch glass.

questions.stem: Two dark minerals both have two cleavage directions. In mineral X they meet at close to 90 degrees; in mineral Y at about 60 and 120 degrees. What are X and Y?
options: X is biotite and Y is olivine
X is olivine and Y is biotite
X is pyroxene and Y is amphibole
X is amphibole and Y is pyroxene
questions.explanation: Pyroxenes have two cleavages at nearly right angles, while amphiboles have two cleavages at about 60 and 120 degrees. Olivine has no good cleavage and biotite has only one, along which it splits into sheets.

questions.stem: Why does granite have large, visible crystals while basalt has very small crystals?
options: Granite cooled quickly at the surface; basalt cooled slowly underground
Granite was squeezed by high pressure, which made its crystals grow larger
Granite contains more iron, and iron minerals always form larger crystals
Granite cooled slowly underground; basalt cooled quickly at the surface
questions.explanation: Magma that cools slowly deep underground gives crystals time to grow, forming coarse-grained intrusive rocks such as granite. Lava cools quickly at the surface, forming fine-grained extrusive rocks such as basalt; grain size depends on cooling rate, not composition.

questions.stem: Which sequence of processes forms a clastic sedimentary rock such as sandstone?
options: Deposition, weathering, cementation, erosion, compaction
Heat, pressure, recrystallisation, uplift, weathering
Weathering, erosion, deposition, compaction, cementation
Melting, solidification, weathering, erosion, deposition
questions.explanation: Rock is broken down by weathering, moved by erosion, laid down as sediment, compacted by the weight of overlying layers and cemented by minerals deposited from groundwater. Heat, pressure and recrystallisation form metamorphic rocks.

questions.stem: Which rock is a non-clastic sedimentary rock?
options: Sandstone of cemented quartz grains
Siltstone of fine rock fragments
Limestone formed from shells
Conglomerate of rounded pebbles
questions.explanation: Non-clastic sedimentary rocks form from chemical precipitation or the remains of organisms, such as limestone from shells and coral, rock salt and coal. Conglomerate, sandstone and siltstone are made of fragments of older rock, so they are clastic.

questions.stem: A granite intrusion heats the shale around it, forming a zone of hard, fine-grained rock without layering. What is this rock and process?
options: Schist, formed by regional metamorphism
Hornfels, from contact metamorphism
Gneiss, formed by regional metamorphism
Slate, formed by contact metamorphism
questions.explanation: Contact metamorphism is driven mainly by heat from a nearby intrusion, with little directed pressure, so the rock recrystallises without foliation, giving hornfels. Slate, schist and gneiss are foliated products of regional metamorphism.

questions.stem: Why do regionally metamorphosed rocks such as schist and gneiss show foliation?
options: Lava flows cooled one on top of another in thin sheets
Heat from a nearby intrusion baked the rock in rings
Directed pressure aligned their minerals in parallel layers
Sediments settled in layers before the rock was cemented
questions.explanation: Regional metamorphism happens over large areas at convergent boundaries, where heat combines with directed pressure that aligns platy minerals such as mica into bands. Sedimentary layering is bedding, not foliation.

questions.stem: Shale is buried ever deeper in a collision zone. Which order of rocks forms as temperature and pressure increase?
options: Schist, then slate, then gneiss
Slate, then gneiss, then schist
Slate, then schist, then gneiss
Gneiss, then schist, then slate
questions.explanation: Increasing metamorphic grade turns shale into fine-grained slate, then schist with visible mica, then banded gneiss. Beyond that the rock may begin to melt, which returns material to the igneous part of the rock cycle.

questions.stem: A rock sample is fine-grained, dark and full of small rounded holes. Which identification is best supported?
options: Mudstone, a fine-grained clastic sedimentary rock
Marble, a metamorphic rock
Vesicular basalt, an extrusive igneous rock
Granite, an intrusive igneous rock
questions.explanation: The holes are vesicles left by gas bubbles in lava that cooled quickly at the surface, and fine grains with a dark colour indicate mafic extrusive rock. Mudstone is fine-grained but has no gas holes, and granite is coarse-grained and pale.

questions.stem: Sample P is non-foliated, made of interlocking crystals and fizzes in dilute acid. Sample Q fizzes but is made of shell fragments. Which identification is correct?
options: P is marble (metamorphic) and Q is limestone (sedimentary)
P is limestone (sedimentary) and Q is marble (metamorphic)
P is quartzite (metamorphic) and Q is chert (sedimentary)
P is granite (igneous) and Q is limestone (sedimentary)
questions.explanation: Both contain calcite, which fizzes in acid, but interlocking recrystallised grains show metamorphism of limestone into marble. Visible shell fragments show the rock has not been recrystallised, so Q is limestone; quartzite and granite do not fizz.

questions.stem: The Pilbara's iron ore deposits formed in banded iron formations. Which process first concentrated the iron?
options: Iron-rich lava from hotspot volcanoes poured across the Pilbara in thick sheets
Rivers carried iron-rich sand from weathered granites and dumped it on beaches
Hot fluids from a nearby granite deposited iron in cracks around the intrusion
Oxygen from early photosynthesis caused dissolved iron in the oceans to settle out
questions.explanation: More than two billion years ago, oxygen released by photosynthesising microbes reacted with iron dissolved in seawater, and iron oxides settled in layers on the sea floor. Later weathering and fluids removed silica from parts of these formations, upgrading them to high-grade ore.

questions.stem: Bauxite, the ore of aluminium, is mined at Weipa on Cape York in Queensland. Which conditions formed this deposit?
options: Metamorphism of buried coal seams, which concentrated aluminium in the hot rock
Long, deep weathering in a warm, wet tropical climate, which leached away other elements
Rapid cooling of aluminium-rich lava erupted at an ancient convergent plate boundary
Evaporation of a shallow inland sea, which left aluminium salts in a thick crust
questions.explanation: Bauxite is a laterite: intense tropical weathering over millions of years dissolves and removes silica and other soluble elements, leaving insoluble aluminium oxides and hydroxides concentrated near the surface. It is a weathering deposit, not an igneous or evaporite one.

questions.stem: The black coal of the Hunter Valley and Bowen Basin formed mainly in the Permian period. Which conditions were needed?
options: Marine plankton settled in deep ocean basins and was then heated into gas
Peat dried out at the surface and was hardened by long exposure to sunlight
Volcanic ash buried forests, and the heat of the ash turned wood into coal
Swamp plants were buried before they decayed, then compressed and heated
questions.explanation: Coal forms from plant material that accumulates in waterlogged swamps, where low oxygen slows decay, and is then buried, compacted and heated over millions of years. Marine plankton is the usual source of oil and gas rather than coal.

questions.stem: Olympic Dam in South Australia contains copper, uranium, gold and silver in iron-oxide-rich broken rock. Which process best explains how such a deposit forms?
options: Hot, metal-rich fluids flowed through fractured rock and deposited minerals as they cooled
Heavy minerals were sorted by waves and concentrated on an ancient beach as placers
Tropical weathering removed soluble elements and left the metals at the land surface
Organic matter in swamp sediments was buried and heated, which concentrated the metals
questions.explanation: Olympic Dam is an iron oxide copper-gold deposit, formed when hot hydrothermal fluids carrying dissolved metals moved through broken rock and precipitated ore minerals. Placer and lateritic weathering deposits form at the surface by quite different processes.

questions.stem: Heavy mineral sands containing zircon, rutile and ilmenite are mined along parts of Australia's coast. How were they concentrated?
options: Coral reefs absorbed the metals from seawater and released them as sand
Waves and currents carried away lighter grains and left the denser minerals behind
Magma intruded the beach sand and crystallised the heavy minerals in place
Seawater evaporated in coastal lagoons and precipitated the heavy minerals
questions.explanation: These are placer deposits: the minerals weathered out of inland rocks and were transported to the coast, where waves and currents winnowed out lighter quartz grains and left the dense minerals concentrated.

questions.stem: Major importers of Australian thermal coal plan to cut their coal-fired electricity, while demand for copper is forecast to rise with electrification. What is the most likely long-term economic effect for Australia?
options: Rising export income from thermal coal because supply will become scarce
Falling income from copper because renewable energy needs less wiring
No change in the relative value of either export over the coming decades
Falling export income from thermal coal and growing income from copper
questions.explanation: Lower demand for coal-fired power reduces long-term demand for thermal coal, while wind, solar, transmission lines, batteries and electric vehicles all use large amounts of copper. Projections are uncertain, but the direction of each trend follows from the demand change.

questions.stem: Australia mines bauxite, refines it into alumina and smelts some into aluminium. Why does the smelting stage depend so heavily on cheap, reliable electricity?
options: Alumina is shipped overseas by electric trains, so transport is the largest cost
Aluminium is extracted from alumina by electrolysis, which uses huge amounts of electricity
Aluminium must be stored frozen after smelting, which runs refrigeration constantly
Bauxite is crushed into fine powder by electric mills before it can be smelted
questions.explanation: Aluminium metal is produced by passing a large electric current through molten alumina, so electricity is a major share of a smelter's costs. That is why smelters are sensitive to power prices and are major electricity users.

questions.stem: The tonnage of iron ore Australia exports changes little from one year to the next, yet the income it earns can rise or fall by large amounts. What mainly explains this?
options: Most iron ore is used in Australia, so exports depend on local building
The world iron ore price rises and falls with demand for steelmaking
The ore grade in the Pilbara changes greatly from one year to the next
Iron ore is sold by volume rather than by mass, so its value fluctuates
questions.explanation: Iron ore is sold on a world market, and its price follows demand from steelmakers, mainly in Asia. With similar tonnages shipped, a change in price changes export income almost directly, which is why government revenue forecasts track the iron ore price closely.

questions.stem: Australia exports large volumes of natural gas as liquefied natural gas (LNG), yet it imports most of the petrol, diesel and jet fuel it uses. Which economic impact follows?
options: Fuel imports are paid for in gas, so world oil prices do not affect Australia
Oil and gas are the same product, so exporting gas reduces the need for oil imports
Gas exports earn income, but fuel imports leave Australia exposed to world oil prices
Gas exports set the price of petrol, so local fuel prices stay below world prices
questions.explanation: Natural gas and crude oil are different resources used for different purposes, so gas exports do not replace imported liquid fuels. Australia earns export income from LNG while paying world prices for the transport fuels it imports, so a rise in oil prices raises costs across the economy.

questions.stem: What makes a mineral 'critical' in Australia's critical minerals list?
options: It is found only in Australia and cannot be mined anywhere else in the world
It is radioactive, so its mining and export must be strictly controlled by law
It is essential to modern technologies and its supply chain is at risk of disruption
It is the mineral that earns the most export income for Australia in a given year
questions.explanation: Critical minerals are those vital to economies, technologies and security, such as renewable energy and defence, whose supply could be disrupted. The list is reviewed periodically as technology and markets change, and some listed minerals earn far less than iron ore or coal.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a critical mineral with its main use in a renewable energy economy is correct?
options: Rare earth elements: permanent magnets in wind turbine generators and electric motors
Lithium: the reflective coating on the front of photovoltaic solar panels
Graphite: the steel towers that hold wind turbines high above the ground
Vanadium: the copper wiring that connects solar farms to the grid
questions.explanation: Rare earths such as neodymium make strong permanent magnets used in many wind turbine generators and electric vehicle motors. Lithium and graphite are used mainly in batteries, and vanadium in vanadium flow batteries and steel alloys.

questions.stem: A geologist says a lithium deposit has a large resource but a much smaller reserve. What does this mean?
options: Only part of the known lithium can be mined profitably with current technology
Most of the lithium has already been mined, and only a small amount remains
The lithium is spread across many countries, and only a little is in Australia
The lithium has been set aside by government for future generations to use
questions.explanation: A resource is a concentration of a mineral that could eventually be extracted, while a reserve is the part that can be mined economically now, based on drilling, costs and prices. Reserves can grow as prices rise or technology improves.

questions.stem: Which exploration method collects direct physical evidence of the rock beneath the surface at a prospect?
options: Studying an existing geological map of the area
Diamond drilling to recover a solid core of rock
Satellite imaging of the surface in many wavelengths
An airborne magnetic survey flown over the region
questions.explanation: Drilling recovers actual rock that can be logged and analysed for grade, so it is direct sampling. Remote sensing and airborne geophysics detect properties from a distance and are used to choose targets for drilling, and maps guide where to look.

questions.stem: In a class model of a geomagnetic survey, a magnet is buried under sand and readings are taken on a grid. One grid square gives a sharply higher reading than all its neighbours. What does this indicate?
options: The magnetic body is most likely directly beneath that square
The magnetic body is deepest beneath that square of the grid
The magnetic body must be spread evenly beneath the whole grid
The reading in that square is an error and should be discarded
questions.explanation: A magnetic anomaly is strongest directly above a magnetic ore body such as magnetite, so a sharp local peak marks its likely position. A deeper body gives a weaker, broader anomaly, and a single high value should be checked by repeating it rather than discarded without reason.

questions.stem: Pilbara iron ore lies in large, near-surface bodies. Why is open pit mining used rather than underground mining?
options: Shallow, large ore bodies can be dug out in bulk at a lower cost per tonne
Open pits produce less waste rock and disturb less land than underground mines
Underground mining is not permitted in Western Australia for any type of ore
Open pit mining avoids the need for blasting, trucks and processing of the ore
questions.explanation: Open pit mining suits large ore bodies near the surface: big equipment moves huge tonnages cheaply and most of the ore is recovered. Its drawbacks are a large surface footprint and large volumes of waste rock, so the second claim is the reverse of the truth.

questions.stem: Olympic Dam's ore body lies hundreds of metres below the surface, and the deposit is mined underground. Which comparison with open pit mining best justifies this choice?
options: Underground mining has lower safety risks for workers than open pit mining does
Underground mines need no ventilation or ground support, so they are cheaper
Removing that much overlying rock to reach the ore would cost more than tunnelling to it
Underground mines always recover more of the ore body than open pit mines can
questions.explanation: For a deep ore body, the waste rock that an open pit would need to remove would be enormous, so tunnelling to the ore is more economic and disturbs far less surface land. Underground mining costs more per tonne, needs ventilation and ground support and brings its own safety risks.

questions.stem: Which is a key environmental risk of offshore oil and gas drilling, compared with onshore drilling?
options: Drilling platforms remove large areas of forest for roads and well pads
Saline water produced by the wells is stored in ponds on productive land
A blowout or spill can spread oil across the sea and reach coastlines
Wells must be drilled through farmland and can split up rural properties
questions.explanation: Offshore, a well blowout or pipeline failure can release oil into currents that carry it over large areas of ocean and coast, and clean-up is difficult. Clearing for well pads and roads and storing produced water on land are concerns for onshore fields such as coal seam gas.

questions.stem: Waste rock at a mine contains pyrite (iron sulfide). Rainwater draining from the dump becomes acidic and carries dissolved metals. Which management practice best addresses the cause?
options: Spreading the waste rock thinly over a large area so that rain can wash it more quickly
Crushing the waste rock finely so that the pyrite dissolves before it reaches streams
Spraying the dump with fresh water each day so that the acid is diluted on site
Covering the waste to keep out water and oxygen, and adding limestone to neutralise acid
questions.explanation: Acid mine drainage forms when sulfide minerals react with oxygen and water to produce sulfuric acid. Limiting their contact with air and water, and neutralising any acid formed, tackles the cause; spreading or crushing the rock exposes more sulfide surface and makes it worse.

questions.stem: Fine waste left after ore is processed is pumped into a tailings storage facility. Why is the facility lined and monitored with groundwater bores?
options: To raise the water table so that native plants grow on the tailings
To detect and prevent seepage of contaminated water into groundwater
To recover the remaining ore from the tailings using the monitoring bores
To store fresh water for the town that supplies the mine's workforce
questions.explanation: Tailings can contain residual metals and processing chemicals, so liners reduce seepage and monitoring bores detect any contamination early. Stable dam walls also matter, because a tailings dam failure can release large volumes of waste.

questions.stem: A mine rehabilitates each worked-out section as it goes, rather than waiting until the mine closes. What is the main environmental advantage?
options: No topsoil needs to be stored, because new soil forms on the site
Rehabilitation is no longer needed once the whole mine has closed
The mine can use more water, because revegetated land needs none
Less land is bare at any one time, reducing erosion and dust
questions.explanation: Progressive rehabilitation reshapes, covers and revegetates finished areas while mining continues elsewhere, so the area of exposed ground at any time is smaller. It also lets the company test what works before final closure.
